title: A quantum thermal machine surpassing the classical thermodynamic limit on precision
authors: Simon Sundelin, Ludvig Nordqvist, Khalak Mahadeviya, Vyom Kulkarni, Mohammed Ali Aamir, Mark T. Mitchison, Simone Gasparinetti
abstract: Precision in nonequilibrium processes comes at a thermodynamic cost: suppressing fluctuations generally requires increased dissipation. Thermodynamic uncertainty relations (TURs) make this trade-off quantitative by linking current fluctuations to entropy production in classical stochastic dynamics. In the decade since its discovery, the canonical steady-state TUR and its finite-time generalizations have become a cornerstone of non-equilibrium thermodynamics, constraining the performance of molecular machines and allowing heat dissipation to be inferred from observable fluctuations. Whether the canonical TUR can be violated in a controlled quantum device remains an outstanding experimental question, in part because doing so requires resolving extremely small steady-state currents as well as their fluctuations. Here we experimentally show that steady-state quantum transport can surpass the precision permitted by the canonical TUR. We observe this violation in a superconducting quantum thermal machine coupled to a microwave waveguide acting as a cold bath and to a classical noise source providing an effective infinite-temperature bath. We observe a TUR ratio $Q = 1.71 \pm 0.17$, in violation of the classical bound $Q \geq 2$. Our results demonstrate a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamics, paving the way for quantum thermal devices that achieve enhanced precision at reduced energy cost.
summary: This paper experimentally demonstrates that a superconducting quantum thermal machine can surpass the precision limits imposed by classical thermodynamics, violating the canonical Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation. By measuring current fluctuations and heat dissipation in a superconducting circuit, the authors show a quantum enhancement in performance at reduced energy cost. This work highlights a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum thermodynamic regimes.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quantum mechanics allows for the violation of the classical Thermodynamic Uncertainty Relation (TUR), which constrains the trade-off between precision and energy cost in non-equilibrium processes.
main_result: The authors experimentally demonstrated a violation of the classical TUR in a superconducting quantum thermal machine, measuring a ratio $Q = 1.71 \pm 0.17$, which is below the classical bound of $Q \geq 2$.
method: The experiment uses near-quantum-limited heterodyne detection on a superconducting quantum thermal machine to measure the mean photon current and its fluctuations, allowing for the extraction of the TUR ratio $Q$.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting quantum thermal machine built from two flux-tunable transmon qubits forming an artificial molecule, coupled to a cold microwave waveguide bath and driven by classical noise.
key_observables: TUR Ratio ($Q$), mean photon current ($J$), and the diffusion coefficient ($D$) extracted from the Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the outgoing microwave field.
important_parameters: The measurement is performed at dilution refrigerator temperatures ($T < 10 	ext{ mK}$); the classical bound is $Q \geq 2$.
main_assumptions: The classical TUR assumptions (classical Markovian dynamics obeying local detailed balance) are assumed to break down in the quantum regime; the analysis relies on input-output theory and heterodyne detection techniques.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture, the transport cycle, the PSD of the output field showing emission peaks, and plots showing the measured TUR ratio $Q$ versus drive strength.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical context of TURs, details the superconducting quantum thermal machine setup, describes the measurement protocol using heterodyne detection to extract current and noise moments, and finally presents the experimental measurement showing the violation of the classical bound.
why_interesting: This work provides a direct, measurable experimental test of fundamental quantum thermodynamic principles, demonstrating a quantum enhancement in precision beyond classical limits, which is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum thermodynamics.
